articles.title: 'Bhookh itni hai, pet bharta hi nhi': PM Modi pulls up industrialists over lack of jobs, low pay despite tax cuts
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday took a swipe at industry leaders over inadequate job creation or salary hikes despite government
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday took a swipe at industry leaders over inadequate job creation or salary hikes despite government concessions, saying, "How much ever you give, their [India Inc] appetite is never satisfied."Addressing the annual general meeting and convention of FICCI in New Delhi, PM Modi questioned whether companies had raised employee salaries or expanded their workforce.He cited government measures to improve the business environment, including reducing the basic corporate tax rate from 30% in 2014 to 22%, simplifying tax returns and refunds, and cutting GST rates on several products."I know you won't applaud. I know that very well, because your appetite is so enormous that no matter how much you are given, it is never enough (aapki bhookh itni hai, kitna hi khilao pet bharta hi nahi)," he told industry leaders.Referring to the income-tax relief for individuals earning up to Rs 12 lakh annually, PM Modi asked, "I have given income tax relief up to Rs 12 lakh. But have you increased the salaries of your employees? Have you increased the number of employees? No! It is always: 'Modi ji, you do it; we will see what happens.' This is how things will continue."He also referred to the income-tax exemption for annual incomes of up to Rs 12 lakh, saying the relief had boosted people's purchasing power."How much ever you give, their appetite is never satisfied," PM Modi told the industry leaders and urged them do more for their employees instead of expecting the government to shoulder the responsibility for growth.Further recalling an interaction with Income Tax Department officials in Gujarat around 2001-02, when he was chief minister, PM Modi said he had questioned the approach of treating taxpayers as potential wrongdoers."I did not understand much at the time; I had little knowledge and no experience either. But I delivered a speech there. This must have been around 2001-02, perhaps 25 years ago. All the senior officials of the Income Tax Department were present. I asked them: 'When will you stop treating everyone as a thief? What kind of approach is this? You, too, work for the country. Are we the only ones who have taken it upon ourselves to serve the nation? You also do your bit, and every citizen does their bit. Everyone deserves respect,'" he said.'Meri mat suno, par Gandhi kih toh mano'The Prime Minister also invoked Mahatma Gandhi's call for self-reliance and (Swadeshi) indigenous goods, saying the message remained relevant even a century later.Referring to Gandhi's 1930 message, PM Modi questioned why industry still needed to be reminded of the importance of Swadeshi and self-reliance."Imagine, 100 years have passed, but in 1930, Gandhi left us with this message, and today, so many years later, I too have to say the same thing. Is this your success or your failure? Don't listen to me; at least you could have to listen to Gandhi! (Meri mat mano, par Gandhi kih toh mano bhai). He too spoke of Swadeshi before leaving; he too spoke of Atmanirbhar Bharat (Self-Reliant India). And now you have turned 100 years old, yet things remain right where they were ... Spread my message too to every home!" he said.'Don't treat 140 crore Indians as assured market'PM Modi also urged businesses not to take India's large domestic market for granted, saying companies must focus on product quality and compete with international standards."Do not consider the 140 crore Indians an assured market," he said, questioning the mindset that whatever companies produce will automatically find buyers in India.He criticised the practice of marketing certain products as "export quality" for overseas consumers, asking whether Indian customers did not deserve the same standards. "My countrymen deserve quality," he said.The Prime Minister called on businesses to invest in understanding consumer preferences in different markets, develop products suited to local requirements and build distribution networks overseas."Our domestic market should not be our comfort zone. It should give us the confidence to compete in global markets," he said.Urges industry to tap trade agreementsPM Modi said India's trade agreements with several countries had opened up major international markets for domestic businesses and asked industry leaders whether they had drawn up plans to make use of the opportunities."Over the past few years, India has entered into trade agreements with several countries around the world. Have you, the members of FICCI, ever sat down to reflect on this? When free trade agreements are signed with major global economies, it means that doors have been opened for you. Have you devised any plans to seize these opportunities, or will I have to come to you to address this as well?" he said.He urged companies to look beyond the domestic market, meet international standards and strengthen their presence in overseas markets.India is 'pharmacy of the world'PM Modi specifically asked the pharmaceutical industry to reduce its dependence on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), bulk drugs and drug intermediates.Pointing out that India is known as the "pharmacy of the world", he said the country continued to import billions of dollars' worth of these products every year."India is called the ‘pharmacy of the world,’ yet it imports billions of dollars' worth of APIs, bulk drugs, and drug intermediates every year. There are hundreds of categories in which we currently depend on imports. Our pharmaceutical industry must understand which ingredients we can manufacture in India. In which areas can we invest in new technology and large production plants to become competitive with other countries?" he said.He called for investment in technology and large-scale manufacturing facilities to build domestic capacity and make Indian companies more competitive globally.'This is a government of friends'PM Modi also asked industry representatives to share their concerns and suggestions for further reforms, saying the government was open to feedback from businesses.Taking a swipe at previous governments, he said the industry's past experiences had affected its relationship with the current administration."Your experience with previous governments has been so bitter that I am having to bear the consequences. This is not the old government; this is a government of friends. It knows how to honour friendship, and you are my true friends. So, without hesitation or reservation, please write to me openly about what still needs to be improved," he said.He added that the government was willing to consider suggestions from industry and urged business leaders to communicate their requirements directly to him.The Prime Minister also said India's progress depended on recognising the contribution of different sections of society, including farmers, entrepreneurs, industries, wealth creators and taxpayers.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Himachal minister stokes row with Op Sindoor remarks; BJP says remarks echo Pakistan's language
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Himachal Pradesh minister Jagat Singh Negi triggered a controversy on Thursday after he said that India had a \"tough time\" dealing with
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Himachal Pradesh minister Jagat Singh Negi triggered a controversy on Thursday after he said that India had a "tough time" dealing with Pakistan during Operation Sindoor.During the assembly session, the BJP moved an adjournment motion to hold a debate on corruption. While addressing the House, Negi alleged massive corruption in the procurement of Rafale fighter jets, claiming India paid Rs 2,300 crore per aircraft instead of Rs 700 crore. Negi also alleged that the fighter jets "proved useless" and resulted in India "having a tough time dealing with Pakistan"."The biggest threat facing India today is corruption and the misuse of public money. That has always been a concern. Let me give you an example of corruption. An aircraft was supposed to be bought for Rs 700 crore. It was called Rafale, a very good aircraft. You bought it for Rs 2,300 crore. That is where corruption took place, because it wasn't made of silver," Negi said."And did that Rafale aircraft give Pakistan a tough time during Operation Sindoor? Instead, we were the ones who were left struggling," he added.Reacting to Negi's remarks, the BJP slammed the Himachal Pradesh minister and Congress, saying that such remarks proved that politics takes precedence over the nation for the grand old party."Congress minister Jagat Singh Negi's statement in the state assembly is extremely unfortunate and condemnable. By making such remarks about Operation Sindoor and the valour of the Indian Army, Congress has once again proved that for the party, politics takes precedence over the nation and the respect due to its soldiers," the BJP wrote in a social media post on X."Why is it that whenever the country's security and the valour of its armed forces are discussed, Congress's statements appear to echo Pakistan's language?" the party added.Himachal Pradesh leader of opposition Jairam Thakur also slammed Negi, terming his remarks absurd and irresponsible. He also urged the Speaker of the assembly to expunge his remarks from the official record."Jagat Singh Negi is known for making absurd and irresponsible statements, both inside and outside the Legislative Assembly. I fail to understand why a minister of such seniority uses such language. Yesterday, during a discussion in the Assembly, he made a very serious remark regarding the Indian Armed Forces. When one of our colleagues from the opposition pointed out to the ruling party MLAs that the Rafale fighter jets had dealt a crushing blow to the Pakistani military, Negi responded by claiming that it was not the Indian Armed Forces or the Rafale jets that had achieved this, but rather that the Indian Armed Forces themselves had been the ones to suffer a crushing defeat," Thakur said."This is recorded in the assembly proceedings. We strongly oppose this and have urged the Speaker of the assembly to ensure that these remarks are expunged from the official record," he added.BJP MLA Rakesh Jamwal also attacked Negi and said, "The way he uses language inside the assembly is concerning... He raised matters against the PM Modi-led Central government. He even questioned the country's armed forces. He made baseless remarks about Operation Sindoor and said that Rafale jets were purchased at high prices, adding that Pakistanis should have died, but Indians were losing their lives."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Bring them back': To end terror, Amit Shah pushes to hunt down fugitives hiding abroad
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Thursday called for bringing offenders hiding abroad back to India, saying it was essential to completely
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Thursday called for bringing offenders hiding abroad back to India, saying it was essential to completely eliminate terrorism, organised crime and drug-related problems.Addressing the inaugural session of the two-day Anti-Terror Conference organised by the National Investigation Agency (NIA) in New Delhi, Shah said tackling these threats required coordinated action against criminal networks operating beyond India's borders.He stressed the need to strengthen efforts to track down and bring back offenders who continue to evade Indian law enforcement agencies from foreign locations.Shah's remarks come amid the government's broader push to dismantle the networks linking terrorism, organised crime and drug trafficking. Offenders operating from abroad can continue to coordinate criminal activities, facilitate cross-border trafficking and maintain links with associates in India, making international cooperation and extradition crucial to tackling such networks.The home minister also cited the dismantling of the Popular Front of India (PFI) network as a significant example of coordinated operations by police forces across the country. He said cooperation among state police forces and central agencies was crucial to effectively tackle networks that operate across state boundaries.The Centre banned the PFI and its affiliates for five years under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) in September 2022, citing their alleged links to terrorist activities, terror financing and other unlawful acts. The ban followed coordinated nationwide searches and arrests carried out by the National Investigation Agency (NIA), Enforcement Directorate (ED) and state police forces.On Jammu and Kashmir, Shah said the Valley was now free of locally recruited terrorists following the killing of Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) operative Lateef Bhat. He credited the security forces and intelligence agencies for the operation, describing it as a significant milestone in efforts to eliminate local terror recruitment.The two-day conference, being held on November 19 and 20, is centred on the theme of cross-border terrorism. Organised by the NIA, it brings together state police forces, central agencies and experts to discuss intelligence sharing, obtaining evidence from foreign jurisdictions, digital forensics, terror financing and countering radicalisation.The conference is also focusing on strengthening the investigation and prosecution of terror-related cases, including the use of digital evidence, trial management and witness protection. It aims to improve coordination between central agencies and state police forces and build their capacity to respond to emerging security threats.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A London professor claimed his neighbour made his £680,000 flat unsellable by revealing past property disputes to a buyer; he lost his £80,000 claim and faced a £180,000 legal bill
articles.summary: A London professor and his wife ended up facing a legal bill of around £180,000 after a dispute with their neighbour over the sale of their flat.
articles.body: A London professor and his wife ended up facing a legal bill of around £180,000 after a dispute with their neighbour over the sale of their flat. Professor Daslav Brkic had sought £80,000 in damages from Douglas Palin, claiming that his disclosures about their past property disagreements had put off prospective buyers and made their £680,000 home difficult to sell.According to The Independent, the case went to trial for a week before Judge Nigel Gerald dismissed the claim. The judge found that Palin was entitled to share factual information with a prospective buyer and that there was insufficient evidence that his disclosures had caused the buyer to withdraw. Brkic and his wife were ordered to pay Palin's estimated £45,000 legal costs, in addition to their own expenses of about £135,000.What led to the neighbours' long-running property disputeBrkic and his wife bought the ground-floor and garden apartment in a Victorian building in Alexandra Grove, Finsbury Park, in 2013. Palin, a wine retailer, owned the freehold and lived in an upper-floor flat. The couple undertook extensive refurbishment, which led to disagreements with Palin. These included disputes over flooring, windows, burglar bars and electrical cabling.In 2021, Palin took the couple to a tribunal over their removal of carpets, which breached the lease. The tribunal ruled in Palin’s favour, and the couple later had the flat re-carpeted to address noise nuisance. The ruling went against Palin in a separate tribunal hearing over repeated inspections. The disagreements continued as the couple prepared to sell.Why did Brkic blame Palin after a second buyer withdrew the offerThe couple decided to sell the flat in 2023. A £680,000 offer fell through early that year, while another buyer withdrew in August after offering about £640,000. Brkic blamed Palin for the second failed sale. He argued that Palin had included a list of complaints in a Leasehold Property Enquiries form supplied during the sale process. The disclosures referred to the resolved carpet dispute, earlier disagreements over windows and burglar bars, and a bathroom issue. The leasehold plan appeared to place part of the bathroom on Palin’s property, although this was later described as a mistake. Brkic’s barrister argued that most matters had already been resolved and should not have been raised.The judge found no evidence that the disclosures caused the sale to failPalin told the court that the matters he disclosed were genuine concerns. Replacing sash windows in a Victorian property with UPVC could affect the value of the building as a whole. His barrister argued that he was entitled to make the disclosures and had acted prudently. Judge Gerald agreed that Palin had acted within his rights when completing the questionnaire. He said the form set out matters of historical fact and found no suggestion that Palin had acted dishonestly or in bad faith. The judge found no sufficient evidence that the information was the material or sole cause of the buyer’s withdrawal. The purchasers appeared to have withdrawn before receiving Palin’s comments.Couple ordered to pay neighbour’s legal costs after claim was dismissedThe judge also rejected the argument that Palin’s disclosures had made the flat unsellable on the open market. By August 2024, all issues apart from cooking odours and electrical cabling had been formally resolved. He said he struggled to understand why the property could not be sold in those circumstances.The court also heard that Brkic and his wife had not disclosed some issues in their own property and leasehold information forms. Judge Gerald dismissed their claim and ordered them to pay Palin’s legal costs, estimated at £45,000. They were told to pay £30,000 within 28 days. The couple’s own legal costs were about £135,000, taking their total bill to approximately £180,000.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available reports. The Times of India has not independently verified the details of the property dispute, the claims made by either party, or the court proceedings.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Russell Brand's prison message remains on YouTube despite U.K. government calls for it to be deleted
articles.summary: The comedian asked supporters to support his family after he was sentenced to more than 10 years for rape and sexual assault.
articles.body:
Google has reportedly refused a request by the British government to remove a YouTube video in which the wife of convicted rapist Russell Brand reads out a statement he gave to her from inside prison, claiming he is innocent.

The U.K.'s Ministry of Justice confirmed it is investigating whether Brand broke prison rules on making public statements, while a spokesperson told the BBC it was "only right" to ask for content that is "distressing for victims" to be taken down from the platform.

Former comedian and actor Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Nov. 9 after being found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three more between 2004 and 2009.

In a YouTube video posted on Sunday, Laura Brand read a statement from her husband in which he maintained his innocence and urged supporters to help his "treasured wife and family."

The Guardian reported Thursday that Google had rejected calls to delete the video, which was still live as of 9 a.m. Nov 19.

A Google spokesperson previously told the outlet, "We're aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube partner program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetize on YouTube since then."

An MOJ spokesperson told Yahoo News, "It is only right that the Government asks for content that is distressing for victims to be taken down, and we strongly believe YouTube should remove this content. Removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms."

In response to the video, a woman who accused Brand of raping her when she was 16 condemned it, calling it an "insult" to his victims and questioning why YouTube had allowed the video to be shared.

Mia Latter told the U.K.'s The Jeremy Vine Show , "I was shocked that YouTube put it out, because I feel like they have some kind of responsibility not to let these things be broadcast.

"And it was an insult to all the women that stood trial, and it was an insult to the jurors that gave their time. It's an insult to the criminal justice system."

British news outlets have since reported that Brand risks losing prison privileges and having his calls restricted if an investigation finds his message broke the rules.

U.K. Justice Secretary Alex Norris said on Nov. 16 in a post on X : "The broadcast of a statement from Russell Brand is completely unacceptable. Prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims. This is being urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules."

An official spokesperson for the U.K. prime minister, Andy Burnham, said Monday that Brand's statement was "clearly appalling," adding that Burnham expects "action to be taken if he's found to have broken the rules."

Ed Miliband, the U.K. foreign secretary, told Sky News that it was "disgusting" that Brand showed "no remorse, no sympathy for the victims."

Brand's YouTube channel has 6.6 million subscribers. Before he was sentenced, he posted weekly episodes of Sunday Service with the Brands , a podcast he hosted with his wife.

Brand said in the statement that he had been moved to HMP Littlehey, a lower-security prison in Cambridgeshire, England. He was previously held at HMP Wandsworth, a high-security facility in London, before being transferred over the weekend, according to the BBC .

The move reportedly followed concerns for Brand's safety. The Times of London reported that he had been held in isolation at Wandsworth to protect him from potential attacks by other prisoners.

HMP Littlehey is a "Category C" prison in the U.K., meaning prisoners are considered unlikely to attempt escape but are not deemed suitable for an "open prison," the lowest-security category. Inmates are also provided with training and opportunities to develop their own skills to help them resettle in the community upon release.

Brand is expected to serve two-thirds of his prison sentence before being eligible for release.

In the clip, Laura Brand reads out a statement from her husband in which he references God and thanks those who have supported him.

He goes on to say that he is innocent of the crimes for which he has been found guilty.

He describes the staff at HMP Littlehey as "strong," "kind" and "dedicated," before going on to ask those listening to "support my treasured wife and family."

Latter was one of the women who featured in a 2023 joint investigation into Brand conducted by U.K. newspapers the Sunday Times and the Times and the TV broadcaster Channel 4. She was known under the pseudonym "Alice" but has recently waived her right to anonymity. She did not feature in the recent trial against Brand, who previously denied all allegations contained in the 2023 report.

Since the verdict, six more women have accused Brand of sexual misconduct , according to a separate investigation by the Times and Sunday Times newspapers in London. The claims made by the women, who all spoke under pseudonyms, span the period from 2005 to 2015.

Delivering the sentence earlier this month at Southwark Crown Court, a criminal court in London, judge Joel Bennathan said Brand had acted with a "casual and arrogant disregard."

He said: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say 'no' and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent."

Yahoo News has reached out to Google for comment.

articles.title: Bihar CM's security 'pushes' Nishant Kumar; JD(U) demands action, police calls it 'human error'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Janata Dal (United) on Thursday took exception to Bihar chief minister Samrat Chaudhary's security staff allegedly pushing health minister
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Janata Dal (United) on Thursday took exception to Bihar chief minister Samrat Chaudhary's security staff allegedly pushing health minister Nishant Kumar during an official visit to Vaishali district.JD(U) MLC Neeraj Kumar urged Bihar Police to take cognisance of the footage and initiate appropriate action."The video that has surfaced is absolutely disheartening. Police headquarters should seriously initiate proceedings to ascertain whether that was a deliberate move," he told reporters."Nishant Kumar is the minister in charge of Vaishali and went there with the CM to review preparations ahead of PM Modi's visit. Such an act against him is a matter of concern for everyone," he added.This comes after a video of the incident went viral on social media. The video shows a security personnel pushing the health minister back as he walks behind Chaudhary during a review of preparations for Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to the district.Meanwhile, Neeraj also warned that those spreading a false narrative on social media would not be spared."The combination of Nishant Kumar and Samrat Choudhary is remarkable. There is no question of disrespecting him," he said.Senior JD(U) leader and minister Ashok Choudhary, however, sought to play down the incident, saying the security personnel might not have noticed Nishant Kumar."He did not push him intentionally. I believe no security personnel will do such a thing intentionally to Nishant Kumar, or for that matter, any other minister," he said.What Bihar Police saidMeanwhile, Bihar Police's Special Security Group, which provides protection to the chief minister, described the incident as a case of "human error".In a statement, the SSG said an inquiry found that the incident occurred due to human error while its personnel were following security protocols for the chief minister.The SSG also noted that it had provided security to Nishant Kumar for nearly two decades until a few months ago.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Zeynab Javadli, ex-wife of Dubai prince Sheikh Saeed bin Maktoum, alleges UAE officials assaulted and drugged her before taking away her three daughters; approaches UN seeking investigation
articles.summary: A bitter custody battle involving Dubai's royal family has taken a fresh turn, with Zeynab Javadli approaching the United Nations for help after allegedly
articles.body: A bitter custody battle involving Dubai's royal family has taken a fresh turn, with Zeynab Javadli approaching the United Nations for help after allegedly being assaulted and drugged by UAE officials during a raid at her home. The former wife of Dubai prince Sheikh Saeed bin Maktoum bin Rashid Al Maktoum claims that armed officers entered her residence in June 2026, took her three daughters from their beds and left her without access to the children.Javadli, a former international gymnast and Azerbaijan national, says she has not seen her daughters since that night. The children, Sheikha Sanaa, 10, Sheikha Asia, 8, and Sheikha Salama, 7, were allegedly taken away by officers during the operation.The case has taken another legal turn as Javadli is due to stand trial in Dubai on Thursday, November 19, facing charges of kidnapping her own children.In a video message to the United Nations Human Rights Council, she spoke about the traumatic experience and the last moments she remembers with her daughters. "The last thing my girls saw was their mother beaten and drugged on the floor of our home. The last thing I heard was their screams," she said.Legal team asks United Nations to investigate UAE officialsAccording to a report by the Daily Mail, Javadli's British lawyer, David Haigh, has confirmed that human rights barrister Rodney Dixon KC submitted a formal request to the United Nations on Wednesday. The application seeks intervention to establish the whereabouts and welfare of the three children.Dixon has also approached Dr Pau Perez-Sales, the UN's lead investigator on torture, requesting an investigation into Javadli's arrest, detention and alleged treatment by security officials in June 2026.Her legal team claims she was beaten, injected with drugs and detained by State Security for six days without access to a lawyer. She was allegedly interrogated while blindfolded and compelled to record a video confession under duress.This is the second time Javadli has taken her allegations to the United Nations. In October 2022, Dixon had submitted a complaint on her behalf, accusing Dubai authorities of harassment, intimidation and abuse during her custody dispute with Sheikh Saeed.Haigh alleged that following the earlier complaint, Javadli was told to stop discussing the matter publicly and withdraw her allegations. According to him, she was offered the assurance that she could retain custody of her daughters if she agreed to remain silent. He claimed that an arrangement remained in place for three years before the June raid.Dubai court had ordered police to take custody of the childrenThe latest confrontation stems from a Dubai court order directing police to take Javadli's three daughters into the custody of their father, Sheikh Saeed. The order reportedly instructed her to "return custody of the minors" to him and stated that "coercive force may be used if necessary".Javadli refused to hand over the children, arguing that an earlier legal agreement with Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Dubai's ruler and Sheikh Saeed's uncle, gave her the right to retain custody.The June operation at her residence was first reported by the Daily Mail. The incident has since become a major point of contention in the ongoing legal dispute between the former couple.Both parents have made serious allegations in custody disputeCourt documents released in November last year shed light on the allegations exchanged between Javadli and Sheikh Saeed.Javadli accused her former husband of causing emotional distress and harm to their daughters. Her allegations included leaving the children without supervision, using inappropriate language around them, depriving them of sleep and driving recklessly.Sheikh Saeed, a 50-year-old businessman and former Olympic clay shooter, rejected her position and accused her of refusing to follow previous court orders. He alleged that she wanted to keep the children away from him and raise them with what he described as "Western behaviour that does not befit Muslims, citizens of the UAE, and members of the Ruling Family in particular".Haigh has also alleged that Javadli has been made homeless, prevented from accessing the property provided to her by the Ruler's office and placed under a fresh travel ban. She is now facing kidnapping charges over the custody of her daughters, along with cybercrime charges linked to social media posts in which she sought international help.Dubai royal family has faced other high-profile casesThe case has revived attention on previous controversies involving women from Dubai's ruling family.Princess Haya, the former wife of Sheikh Mohammed, left the UAE in 2019 and sought refuge in the UK, where she told the court that she feared for her safety.In another widely reported case, Princess Latifa, Sheikh Mohammed's daughter, released videos in 2021 alleging that she had been drugged and held captive in a villa after attempting to escape Dubai. She later issued a statement saying that she was living as she wished.Princess Shamsa, another daughter of Sheikh Mohammed, was reportedly abducted from a street in Cambridge in August 2000 on her father's orders. She has not appeared in public since.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Musk dumps MAGA after expensive date with Trump Republicans
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent From Washington: Elon Musk is seeking a divorce from MAGA, apparently on grounds of irreconcilable political differences.
articles.body: TOI Correspondent From Washington: Elon Musk is seeking a divorce from MAGA, apparently on grounds of irreconcilable political differences. The man who once boldly declared himself “Dark MAGA,” bankrolled Donald Trump, and wielded the chainsaw of DOGE, is now insisting he was never really one of them.In what is the political equivalent of an uninstallation process, the multi-billionaire boss of SpaceX-Tesla has apparently concluded that being America's unofficial minister for disruption was not quite the career-enhancing investment he imagined. Speaking at The New York Times' DealBook Summit on Wednesday, he initiated a political course correction, describing himself as "quite moderate" and expressing regret at having spent an extraordinary amount of money backing Republican candidates in the midterm elections."Republicans were routed and the money I spent… I feel pretty foolish having spent so much money and not seeing much for it," he confessed. "If I could rewind the clock I would have spent less money."Even for a multi-billionaire, the lolly he splurged was not exactly small beer. Musk reportedly spent approximately $446 million backing Republicans in the 2026 midterms, making him the biggest individual political donor in American electoral history. Much of that money went into trying to preserve GOP dominance in Texas -- where a lot of his tech assets are located -- and in Congress.Voters had other ideas; only three of the nearly 50 candidates he backed won.Pressed about his political identity at the summit, Musk did the tech version of a 404 error not found. "I'm not sure what MAGA means. But if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that," he said.It did not appear so in October 2024, when Musk strode on stage at a Trump rally in Pennsylvania wearing a black MAGA cap and announced, with considerable theatrical passion: "I'm not just MAGA — I'm Dark MAGA." He subsequently became one of Trump's most enthusiastic financial backers, was rewarded with a prominent place in the president's inner circle and took charge of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), the administration's controversial cost-cutting operation. For months, he was a permanent fixture in the White House, turning up in the Oval Office, attending cabinet meetings and helping wield the administration's chainsaw against federal agencies and government employees.It was an extraordinary political journey for a man who once cultivated the image of a freewheeling entrepreneur above party politics. But the romance eventually soured. Musk and Trump had a spectacular public falling-out in 2025, before patching things up. Now, following another electoral disaster, Musk appears to be rediscovering his independent streak.There are several possible explanations for this sudden moderation. The most obvious is that losing elections is bad for business, particularly when one has invested nearly half a billion dollars in ensuring the other side loses. The Democrats' sweeping midterm victory has also changed the political geography of Musk's business empire. Texas, where Tesla and SpaceX have established major operations and where Musk has invested heavily, has elected Democrat Gina Hinojosa governor, ending decades of Republican control. Democrats also captured a Senate seat in Texas and made major gains nationally.The new governor could bring greater scrutiny to Musk's sprawling Texas operations, including tax incentives, data-centre expansion and the controversial Starbase project. Musk, however, struck a conciliatory note, describing Hinojosa as a moderate and saying: "Things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."India is no stranger to Musk’s mercurial politics. He has repeatedly expressed admiration for PM Modi, spoken well of Indian professionals, and even backed the H1B visa program. But he has gradually soured on New Delhi, going so far as to suggest the government was favoring Indian business oligarchs in blocking his Starlink venture to protect their monopolies.So while the Musk courtship may yet prove useful to New Delhi for the tech mojo and moolah he can bring, his latest flip is also a reminder that the world's richest man is nobody's ideological soulmate. His loyalties, like his business interests, are decidedly transactional.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: During WWII, Lance Cpl. Frank Bramhall filmed a message for home; about 70 years later, his daughter saw him on screen for the first time and began asking why he had been awarded a medal
articles.summary: Explore the heartwarming story of Lance Corporal Frank Bramhall's message to his daughter during WWII, uncovered 70 years later, revealing his bravery and the emotional toll of combat.
articles.body: For soldiers, messages from loved ones hold a special place in their hearts. Likewise, messages servicemen sent home were deeply valued by their families. In 2016, Oxford Scientific Films joined hands with the Imperial War Museum and Manchester’s North West Film Archive to create a 1 x 60’ special titledMessages Home: Lost Films of the British Army for Channel 4. The film celebrated Britain’s 14th Army by showing the unique messages they filmed for their loved ones.The documentary featured heartwarming video messages from World War II servicemen fighting Japanese forces in Burma and India. Under those conditions, home leave wasn’t an option. Conditions were so severe that letters sometimes never reached their families in Britain. Some men left behind their pregnant wives and young children who would hardly recognize them by the time they returned. Some bid a bittersweet farewell to their companions, not knowing when they would see each other again.Camera crews were sent to film the soldiersWhile fighting for their country, the British soldiers also faced dangers hidden in the jungle. The worst danger was disease. According to Channel 4 press materials for the documentary, 40% of the 14th Army suffered from malaria. Across every thousand troops, 700 contracted one illness or another. Given the low morale, the Ministry of Defence came up with a scheme to give a much-needed boost to the soldiers in the Far East and their families back home. For the cinematic scheme, called Calling Blighty, theysent multiple Army Film and Photographic Unit [AFPU] crews to record the troops in Asia.A total of 391 segments, each running from 10 to 15 minutes, were recorded. Nearly 8,000 men and a few women sent out personal messages to their nearest and dearest. Friends and families in Britain were invited to special cinema screenings to see their loved ones on the big screen. Unfortunately, several of the men featured had died before the films reached home.Lance Corporal Frank Bramhall was awarded a medalThe documentary included messages from a father speaking to his daughter for the first time, a lovelorn gunner yearning for his sweetheart back home, and others. One of those stories involved a soldier named Lance Corporal Frank Bramhall, who sent a message to his daughter, Michele Simpson, and she saw it 70 years later. Michele and her children, Graham and Joanne, were astonished to see him on screen for the first time. At that time, Michele said her father struggled with what would now be described as PTSD (Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder).Michele was determined to uncover the details of her father’s war record and the recognition he received for his service. Frank was awarded the Military Medal (MM) for gallantry and devotion to his duty while serving with the 2nd Battalion, The East Lancashire Regiment in Burma. To find out more, Michele visited her father’s old regiment and heard that he had shown great courage in action. Michele further mentioned that she understood why his combat experiences had so deeply upset her father. She said she believed his religion was a major reason. She recalled that, as a Roman Catholic, he worried about whether he could go to heaven after killing people during the war. After the war, Frank resumed his career as a grocer, while Michele and her family lived on their family farm in Rochdale.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Wisconsin couple who sued their neighborhood association for a fence so their five children could play safely won $200,000, and now they are suing 33 neighbors who never paid their $1,350 share
articles.summary: A backyard fence intended to protect five children has turned into a costly legal dispute in a Wisconsin neighbourhood, with a family now taking its
articles.body: A backyard fence intended to protect five children has turned into a costly legal dispute in a Wisconsin neighbourhood, with a family now taking its homeowners association and dozens of residents back to court. Lisa and Michael Newman of De Pere, Wisconsin, secured a $200,000 settlement after their neighbourhood association refused to let them build a fence around their property. Now, nearly two years after the settlement, the couple is pursuing unpaid contributions from residents who have not paid their assigned share. The latest development was reported by Realtor dot com and NBC 26, which have followed the dispute since it first reached federal court. The original disagreement began in 2019, when the Newmans approached the Nazcr Trac Property Owners Association (NTPOA) seeking permission to install a fence around their backyard. The couple wanted a secure outdoor space where their five children, all diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, could play without the risk of wandering away.Some of the children had additional medical complexities, and the family believed a fenced yard would make outdoor activities safer while allowing them greater independence. However, the association rejected their request, citing a restrictive covenant dating back to the subdivision’s 2001 plat map, which prohibited fences of any kind. The family subsequently sought legal assistance from Disability Rights Wisconsin and filed a federal lawsuit against the association in August 2021, alleging disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Amendments Act.In May 2022, US District Judge William Griesbach granted the family a preliminary injunction preventing the association from enforcing its no-fence rule against them. The decision allowed the Newmans to finally install the fence, approximately three years after their initial request. The legal battle, however, continued beyond the construction of the backyard barrier.A $200,000 settlement divided among homeownersIn August 2024, the Newmans and the association reached a settlement requiring NTPOA to pay the family $200,000. The financial responsibility was distributed among the neighbourhood’s property owners, with each household expected to contribute $1,350 towards the settlement.The arrangement did not sit well with everyone in the subdivision. Several residents later told NBC 26 that they had not been consulted about the original fence dispute and were unhappy about being asked to contribute towards a legal settlement involving a decision made by the association’s board. Some homeowners also maintained that they would have supported the family’s request had they been given an opportunity to express their views before the matter escalated.According to the Newmans’ attorney, Victoria Davis Dávila, 69 homeowners have settled their outstanding contributions. However, 55 homeowners still owe money, prompting the family to initiate another legal proceeding this autumn.Thirty-three neighbours named in the new lawsuitThe latest lawsuit names the property owners’ association and 33 residents who have not paid their assigned contributions. The distinction is important because the 55 figure represents the number of homeowners the family’s attorney says still owe money, while 33 residents are named in the new filing.The Newmans are seeking to enforce the outstanding payment obligations rather than revisit the original dispute over the fence. The development has once again unsettled residents, particularly those who have already paid their $1,350 share. Some homeowners fear that if the association cannot recover the remaining money, the entire membership could potentially face further financial liability.The association has filed an answer and affirmative defence dated November 16, 2026, according to Realtor dot com. The contents of the filing were not publicly available when the publication reported on the case.A neighbourhood still dividedThe renewed legal action has brought back tensions among residents of Nazcr Trac, with some questioning why individual homeowners should bear the financial consequences of decisions made by the association’s former leadership. For the Newmans, however, the dispute stems from a request they made to provide their children with a safer environment at home. Their attorney has indicated that the family wants the outstanding settlement obligations resolved so everyone involved can move on.What began as a disagreement over a neighbourhood’s restrictions on backyard fencing has consequently developed into a much larger dispute involving disability accommodation, homeowners’ association responsibilities and the financial obligations of residents. articles.title: After years of selling used clothes, Rose Blumkin saved $500 and opened a furniture store in Omaha in 1937; it grew into a retail business acquired by Berkshire Hathaway in 1983
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable journey of Rose Blumkin, who turned $500 into Nebraska Furniture Mart, one of the largest furniture stores in the US, transforming the retail landscape during the Great Depression.
articles.body: A former second-hand clothing seller, Rose Blumkin turned a profit when American firms were feeling the pressures of the Great Depression. The Russian emigrant used her modest savings of $500 and experience in trade to launch Nebraska Furniture Mart in Omaha, Nebraska and eight years later began the approach that would make her company one of the largest furniture outlets in the US.According to Berkshire Hathaway's 1983 shareholder letter, Rose Blumkin’s story caught the attention of billionaire Warren Buffett. It showed how perseverance, aggressive pricing, and customer trust can turn a small operation into a retail giant. Known to many customers as Mrs B. Blumkin, she lacked formal business education and financial training, but she benefited from years of direct selling experience, an eye for customers' needs, and competing against big-name retailers. As it turned out, her story was an important part of Berkshire Hathaway's history after Buffett bought a majority stake in Nebraska Furniture Mart in 1983.From selling used clothes to opening a furniture storeBorn Rose Gorelick in 1893 in a small village near Minsk, Russia, Blumkin grew up in a modest family. She started working early and gained retail experience in the family business. She came to the United States in 1919 to be with her husband, Isadore Blumkin, and ultimately settled in Omaha. The family business focused on the sale of second-hand clothing. Their experience in the business made her realise that it was difficult to attract customers when the economy was poor. She realised that people needed affordable prices rather than high markups to tempt them to buy when the family's budget was tight.Her technique proved especially effective during the great depression. She tried promotional deals and direct mail and ran a promotion: promising to outfit a man from head to toe for $5. The promotion garnered a lot of interest and showed the capacity for gaining customers. By 1937, she had accumulated $ 500 and launched her foray into the furniture business. Opening her first store in a basement in Omaha that she called Nebraska Furniture Mart. It was only a small store to start, but her plan was not limited to a small local operation.A low-price strategy that challenged established retailers Blumkin based her firm’s business plan on a simple philosophy: to sell customers high-quality merchandise at a reasonable price without being disconnected. It is reported that she marked up prices below those of the local furniture stores so that customers could buy furniture and appliances at an affordable rate. This strategy, however, was not without problems. The big furniture retailers did not like the low prices she set on her furniture, and some of the manufacturers pressured her to stop selling their products to their stores. Blumkin replaced these manufacturers and used other routes to buy her products. Her pricing also led to fair-trade violations, which she successfully challenged in court.Her perseverance especially came in the tough times with her business. In the 1983 Buffett shareholder letter, she remembers telling her creditors that she would sell them furniture and appliances from her house if needed. She was more concerned with hering her commitment rather than having a business supported by financial difficulties. The principle can be seen in academic papers and research studies published in the Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services, which analyses how customer and entrepreneurial orientation affect the performance of small retailers.Warren Buffett's 1983 acquisition and the business's legacyBy the early 1980s, Nebraska Furniture Mart had become a retail powerhouse. Warren Buffett, who had long admired Blumkin and her family's capabilities as businesspeople and managers, identified the acquisition as one of the year's highlights in Berkshire Hathaway's 1983 letter to shareholders. Berkshire Hathaway purchased a 90% interest in the company for $55.3 million, while family members retained the remaining 10%. The agreement allowed the Blumkin family to remain involved in the business and maintain its connection with the original owners.Face stated that it was an incredible business. It did more than $100 million in annual sales from a single-store, 2,000-square-foot showroom. It had good buying habits, terrific operations, and passed on savings to customers. She became a widow at age 94 but continued with the business until retiring at the age of 103. In 1998, she died, having built the business into far more than the small basement store she first opened in 1937. Today, Nebraska Furniture Mart operates in Omaha, Des Moines, Kansas City and the Dallas-Fort Worth metro area.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'There is no private individual who has helped Ukraine more than I have': Elon Musk says Russia would have won the war if Ukraine did not have Starlink
articles.summary: Elon Musk has claimed that Russia would have already won its war against Ukraine if Kyiv had not received access to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet
articles.body: Elon Musk has claimed that Russia would have already won its war against Ukraine if Kyiv had not received access to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet network, arguing that the technology has been instrumental in keeping Ukrainian forces connected since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Speaking at The New York Times' DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Musk said Starlink was the only communications system Russia had been unable to disable after its invasion destroyed Ukraine's existing communications infrastructure.“I think it would probably be accurate to say that there is no private individual who has helped Ukraine more than I have,” Musk boasted. “I made sure that Starlink was in Ukraine prepositioned ahead of the Russian invasion.”“And when Russia invaded, they disabled all communications, all cell towers, all fiber cables and every satellite communication system. There was one system they could not disable and that was Starlink.”“If they had not had Starlink, their entire line would have collapsed because they had no communication system and Russia would have won,” he added.The billionaire, who joined the interview remotely, also described his contribution to Ukraine's defence as extraordinary, claiming that no other private individual had helped the country more than he had.“Even to this present day, Starlink provides the backbone of communications for the Ukrainian military and for Ukraine more broadly,” he said.Musk warned that switching off the satellite network would have immediate consequences for Kyiv's military.“If we were to turn off Starlink, the entire Ukrainian front would collapse immediately,” he said, describing SpaceX's contribution as “incredibly supportive of Ukraine”.Musk defends restrictions on Ukraine's Starlink useHis remarks came amid a dispute over restrictions on Ukraine's access to SpaceX's satellite communications systems, which have become critical to its drone warfare capabilities against Russia.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had complained that restrictions on satellite connectivity were affecting military operations, particularly the use of drones and efforts to intercept Russian attacks.During the interview, journalist Andrew Ross Sorkin asked Musk about Zelenskyy's claims that Starshield, the military-grade satellite communications system controlled by the US government, had been affected.Musk rejected the Ukrainian president's account, saying he was referring to the commercial Starlink network rather than Starshield.“That's false. I don't want to blow your mind, but Zelenskyy is not always truthful,” Musk said.He also accused the Ukrainian president of misrepresenting Kyiv's request. “He's lying, and what he is actually saying is he wants to use Starlink for military, offensive military operations,” Musk said.The SpaceX chief insisted that Starlink was designed as a civilian communications service and should not be used for offensive drone strikes. “Starlink is a civilian system. It is not meant to be used for offensive drone strikes that kill people,” he said, adding that such operations should use Starshield, which is controlled by the US government.Musk said he did not want to be personally responsible for decisions that could result in people being killed.“Do not ask me as a private individual to make kill decisions that sometimes result in the loss of innocent lives, not just soldiers. That is not my position to do,” he said.He also said SpaceX had imposed a speed restriction on Starlink terminals, comparing it to Ukraine's highway speed limit of approximately 80 miles per hour (129 kmph). The restriction was intended to prevent the commercial network from being used for offensive military operations, he argued.Musk calls for empathy for Russian soldiersThe billionaire also made controversial remarks about the human cost of the war, urging people to show sympathy for Russian soldiers as well as Ukrainian troops. e argued that Russian soldiers were being conscripted and forced to fight, saying that thousands of young men were being sent to die without any meaningful change in territorial boundaries.“You should have empathy not just for the Ukrainian boys who are dying, but also for the Russian ones because they are conscripted and forced to go to that line,” he said.Musk criticized what he described as a tendency to view Ukraine as entirely good and Russia as entirely bad, arguing that people had become too accepting of violence against Russian soldiers.He acknowledged that Russia was the aggressor in the invasion but also repeated his controversial claim that the US had helped orchestrate the overthrow of Ukraine's former pro-Russian president Viktor Yanukovych. “It is true that we Americans staged a coup to overthrow the democratically elected pro-Russian president of Ukraine,” he claimed, referring to the 2014 political upheaval that led to Yanukovych fleeing the country.Musk denied that his comments amounted to support for Moscow, pointing to SpaceX's role in reducing Russia's access to commercial space launches.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Washington landowner made unpermitted repairs to a dam in 2017; when it failed, water and sediment filled a neighbour's pond, and an appeals court has upheld $554,294.35 in trespass and nuisance damages
articles.summary: A landowner in Washington state carried out repairs on a dam without obtaining the required permit or consulting an engineer.
articles.body: A landowner in Washington state carried out repairs on a dam without obtaining the required permit or consulting an engineer. When the dam failed months later, water and decades of accumulated sediment rushed onto a neighbour's property, filling one pond and damaging another. Nearly nine years after the work, an appeals court has upheld a judgment awarding the neighbour more than $554,000 for trespass and nuisance.The dispute involved Robert Shawn Noecker and the owners of an adjoining property in Bothell, Washington. On November 16, the Washington Court of Appeals, Division One, affirmed the trial court's findings that the dam work and separate drainage alterations had caused unlawful damage to Noecker's land.The court also sent the case back to the lower court to consider whether Noecker should receive additional compensation for emotional distress. It awarded him reasonable attorney fees and costs for the appeal.How the dam failure damaged the neighbouring propertyAccording to the court's opinion available online, the dam had been built in 1981 by a previous owner of the Bernhart property, under a permit from the Washington Department of Ecology. It blocked a natural stream to create a pond and controlled the release of water through a six-inch pipe.The dam also held back sediment that accumulated over the years. Water and sediment were released in a regulated manner onto the neighbouring South Noecker property, where they flowed into two ponds. Noecker had raised concerns about the dam's condition from May 2014 onwards, warning Craig Bernhart that it could fail and cause damage.In 2017, Bernhart undertook repair work. This included installing a new pipe, filling the dam walls with soil and compacting it using the shovel of a backhoe. The court noted that Bernhart contacted the Department of Ecology but did not obtain a permit or permission for the work. He also did not consult an engineer.The work did not meet industry standards, according to the court's findings. In October 2017, the dam failed, creating a large opening through which much of the stored water escaped. The breach released large quantities of sediment that had accumulated behind the structure over approximately 40 years.The water flowed towards Noecker's property, completely filling its upper pond with sediment. The lower pond also began filling and was expected to be completely filled if the damage continued. Snohomish County Planning and Development Services issued a stop-work order on October 6, 2017, and a notice of violation on October 9 over the unpermitted work.Separate drainage work also sent water onto his landThe court case involved another set of alterations made in 2017. Bernhart had dug drainage ditches to connect the northern part of his property to an existing ditch on Noecker's North property. The new channels artificially collected and redirected water towards Noecker's land. This increased the volume and speed of water flowing onto the property, particularly during heavy rainfall.The excess water and sediment clogged the pump in Noecker's retention pond and caused standing water to collect around his workshop. The court noted that the drainage work had been carried out without the necessary Snohomish County land-disturbance permit. It also found that Bernhart had failed to take steps to prevent harm to the neighbouring property. A contractor who assessed the work described it as poorly executed and said it had caused avoidable damage.Why the appeals court upheld the damagesNoecker filed a lawsuit alleging trespass, negligence, nuisance and statutory waste. The case went to a bench trial in August 2024, meaning a judge rather than a jury heard the evidence.In January 2025, the trial court found in his favour. It awarded $554,294.35 for trespass and nuisance, along with separate damages under Washington's statutory waste law, costs and attorney fees. It also issued an injunction preventing further unlawful water discharge or interference with his property.Bernhart challenged the findings, arguing that the water diversion did not amount to trespass or nuisance and that the court had wrongly rejected legal defences available to landowners dealing with surface water. The Court of Appeals rejected those arguments. It found that the drainage channels had artificially collected and redirected water in a way that differed from its natural flow and caused substantial damage.The judges also concluded that the dam repairs had been carried out without the required permit and that the resulting water and sediment flow continued to damage Noecker's property.The court said the trial judge had sufficient evidence to conclude that the work amounted to trespass and nuisance. It therefore affirmed the $554,294.35 award for those claims. The judgment also records separate awards of $72,051.84 for statutory waste, $144,103.68 in trebled damages under that law, $24,207.62 in costs and $65,457.62 in attorney fees. These are additional amounts and should not be confused with the $554,294.35 awarded for trespass and nuisance.Court sends emotional distress claim back for reviewNoecker had also sought compensation for the anxiety and emotional distress caused by the damage to his property. The trial court had acknowledged that he experienced distress but refused to award damages for it.The appeals court disagreed with that decision. It said emotional distress damages can generally be recovered for intentional torts such as trespass and nuisance. It therefore directed the lower court to reconsider whether Noecker should receive compensation on this ground. The ruling means the original damages award remains in place, while the question of additional compensation for emotional distress is still to be decided.You use AI every day. articles.title: Missouri homeowners paid off a $37,325 property loan, but the original sellers refused to clear the lien and blocked a $272,500 sale; in November 2026, an appeals court upheld $47,500 in damages for interference
articles.summary: Two Missouri homeowners who had paid off a property loan found themselves unable to complete a $272,500 home sale after the original sellers refused to
articles.body: Two Missouri homeowners who had paid off a property loan found themselves unable to complete a $272,500 home sale after the original sellers refused to release a lien on the property. The sellers claimed that money was still owed, but the homeowners maintained that they had completed all payments years earlier. The dispute eventually led to a lawsuit over the failed sale and the sellers' refusal to clear the property's title.On November 17, 2026, the Missouri Court of Appeals upheld a judgment awarding the homeowners $47,500 for tortious interference with a real estate contract. In its opinion in Joseph C Barber and Brenda L Barber v. Kimberly R Weger, the court also affirmed the finding that the $37,325 loan had been fully repaid. The court also remanded the case for the trial court to determine the additional reasonable attorney's fees Kimberly Weger must pay for work after the original judgment and during the appeal, according to the opinion available on Justia.How the property loan and sale dispute beganJoseph and Brenda Barber purchased a property at 4905 West Route F in Clark, Missouri, from Kimberly Weger and her husband, Aubrey, in 2006. They financed part of the purchase through a $37,325 promissory note and signed a deed of trust in favour of the sellers as security for the loan. The deed of trust was recorded in Boone County on November 22, 2006.Under the agreement, the couple had to make monthly payments of $450 from December 2006 through November 2015. A late fee of $25 applied when a payment was not made before the 15th of the month. Brenda later testified that they made the required payments and settled the loan with their final payment in November 2015.In April 2022, the Barbers agreed to sell the property for $272,500, with closing scheduled for May 13. Before the transaction could be completed, they discovered that the deed of trust remained recorded against the property. The Wegers refused to release it, claiming that several payments, particularly those due in 2014 and 2015, had not been received.The sellers also declined to provide a payoff amount. Aubrey told Brenda that she could not sell the property because she did not own it and said he would stop the sale because he wanted the property back. Their son, Ashtin, also told Brenda that he would make sure people knew the couple could not sell it.Why the original sale fell throughThe Barbers hired an attorney, who sent a formal demand in May 2022 asking the Wegers to release the deed of trust and provide the required documentation. The letter included available payment records and money to cover the recording costs. The Barbers also offered to place any disputed balance in escrow so the sale could proceed, but the Wegers continued to refuse to provide a payoff figure or release the lien.The buyers were unwilling to complete the purchase while the deed of trust remained on the property. The Barbers extended the closing date three times and reduced the agreed price to $225,000, but the original sale still failed.They later filed a lawsuit against Kimberly, Aubrey and Ashtin. The claims included a violation of Missouri's law requiring the release of a deed of trust after a secured debt has been paid, as well as tortious interference with a real estate contract. In June 2024, the trial court ordered the deed of trust released. The Barbers subsequently sold the property for $225,000 on September 16, 2024.What the courts decidedDuring the trial, Brenda testified that the loan had been fully paid, supported by bank records for payments made in 2014 and 2015. Kimberly presented records suggesting that only 67 of the 107 required payments had been made. However, some payments shown in the Barbers' bank records were missing from her records.The trial court accepted Brenda's account and ruled in May 2025 that the Wegers had violated the state law governing the release of deeds of trust. It awarded the Barbers $3,732.50 in statutory damages, $28,065.77 in attorney's fees and court costs. It separately awarded them $47,500 for tortious interference with the property sale, while finding in favour of Ashtin on that claim.Kimberly appealed, arguing that the evidence did not establish that the loan was fully paid or that her refusal to release the deed was unjustified. The Court of Appeals rejected both arguments. It found that the trial court was entitled to rely on Brenda's testimony and the supporting bank records. The judges also noted that the sellers had refused to provide a payoff amount despite repeated requests. Evidence showed that their refusal was driven by a desire to prevent the sale and regain an interest in the property, rather than a legitimate claim to unpaid money.The appeals court affirmed the judgment, including the $47,500 award for interference. It also granted the Barbers' request for additional attorney's fees and sent the matter back to the trial court to determine the reasonable amount owed for post-judgment and appellate legal work.You use AI every day. articles.title: A businessman left his daughter nothing in his £1.57 million will after abandoning her when she was eight months old; a court later awarded her £123,418
articles.summary: A daughter who was barely eight months old when her father walked out of her life has secured a share of his estate more than three decades later, despite
articles.body: A daughter who was barely eight months old when her father walked out of her life has secured a share of his estate more than three decades later, despite being specifically excluded from his will. Emma McDaniel was left out of the inheritance arrangements made by businessman Mark Talbot, who had built considerable wealth through business ventures and property investments. The case McDaniel v Talbot & Anor [2026] EWHC 928 (Ch), decided by the High Court on 17 April 2026, reports his estate was worth around £1.57 million when he died in 2022. Although Talbot had made clear that he did not intend to leave anything to his daughter, their relationship had changed in the years before his death. A High Court judge has ruled that Emma should receive £123,418, following a dispute with her stepmother over the inheritance.How Talbot built his fortune through business and propertyMark Talbot separated from Emma's mother in 1985, when their daughter was still a baby. He subsequently had little involvement in her upbringing and never met her younger brother, Rhys, who was born after the separation. Talbot went on to establish a new family with Rosemary, with whom he shared a relationship lasting 36 years. The couple eventually married and had two children together.His professional life took a different course in the years that followed. As per the judgement, Talbot sold a courier business in about 1995, using the proceeds and his subsequent commercial activities to build a substantial financial portfolio. By the time he died, his assets included several rental properties and a villa in Portugal valued at approximately £450,000.A 2014 will remained unchanged after their 2019 reunionTalbot had prepared his will in May 2014, several years before reconnecting with Emma. The document made his intentions towards his two older children explicit, recording that he had not included either of them in his inheritance plans because he had not been in contact with them.Reportedly, he left his estate to Rosemary. The will referred to Emma and Rhys by their previous family surname and explained that he had last seen his daughter approximately 20 years earlier. At the time, the arrangements reflected the distance that had existed between them for much of her childhood and adult life.That position changed in 2019, when Talbot made contact with Emma. The pair began rebuilding their relationship after years apart, eventually developing a close bond. They spoke regularly, spent time together and even went on holidays to his Portuguese property.Their renewed connection lasted only a few years before Talbot died suddenly in 2022, aged 63. He had not revised his will to reflect the relationship that had developed since 2019.Emma's financial circumstances became part of the court caseAt the time of the inheritance dispute, Emma was 40 and raising two children with her husband. Her barrister, Aiden O'Brien, explained to the High Court, "Emma is married with two children, both of whom have a constellation of disabilities. The claimant’s husband also suffers from heart and spinal problems." Emma was dealing with health difficulties of her own, including spinal problems, autism, ADHD, fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue. The family lived in a three-bedroom housing association home and depended on several forms of state assistance to meet their everyday expenses.These included Universal Credit, Personal Independence Payment, Child Benefit and Disability Living Allowance. Income from Emma's small business provided some additional support, but the court heard that the family had little room in its budget for unexpected costs.Her legal team argued that the circumstances justified a claim under inheritance law for reasonable financial provision from her father's estate. Emma was not asking the court to disregard the existence of the will altogether.Stepmother challenged the inheritance claimRosemary opposed the application, maintaining that her late husband's intentions had been clearly expressed in the 2014 document. She argued that he had deliberately chosen not to provide for his older children and that the court should respect that decision.She also disputed the suggestion that Emma's renewed relationship with her father should influence how his estate was divided. Rosemary maintained that the wealth had been built through their joint efforts over many years. According to her case, Talbot's business commitments had restricted her own opportunities to earn and the estate effectively represented her financial security in later life.The proceedings also took an emotional toll on Rosemary. Judge Caroline Shea KC acknowledged that Mark's death had affected both women and referred to the widow's low mood, which had been made worse by the legal proceedings.However, the judge did not accept Rosemary's characterisation of the relationship between Emma and her father as little more than a friendship. Although their reconciliation had taken place relatively late in Talbot's life, the evidence suggested that both had expected it to continue.Judge points to financial need and caring responsibilitiesIn her ruling, Judge Shea considered Emma's financial position alongside the circumstances surrounding her relationship with her father. She described her as a claimant in considerable need, with household resources largely consumed by the cost of supporting herself and her family.The judge observed that Emma could meet ordinary expenses, but doing so left little money for anything beyond basic requirements. Unexpected bills could push the household into debt, while even modest additional spending meant making difficult choices elsewhere.Her decision was also influenced by Emma's involvement in caring for members of the family. This extended beyond the responsibilities she already had towards her own children. The court heard about her contributions to the care of Talbot and his mother, Barbara, both around the period of reconciliation and after his death.Emma had developed a meaningful connection with her father after their reunion and had also maintained a relationship with his mother. The judge considered the nature of those responsibilities when assessing whether the existing inheritance arrangements were fair.She said the provisions governing Talbot's estate had failed to make reasonable financial provision for Emma's maintenance. The relationship between father and daughter, although comparatively brief after their reconciliation, had been genuine and appeared to have been intended as a lasting one.Court awards Emma £123,418 despite her father's willThe judge concluded that Emma's circumstances, her relationship with Talbot and her caring contributions gave her claim a particular weight. She also considered the financial position of Rosemary, finding that the widow had substantial resources of her own in addition to the inheritance she was due to receive. The court determined that making an award to Emma would not leave Rosemary unable to maintain her standard of living or strip her of the greater part of the estate.Emma was consequently awarded £123,418 from her father's £1.57 million estate. The decision meant that, despite the wording of a will that had expressly excluded her, she would receive a financial provision following the High Court proceedings.You use AI every day.
